title: YouTube 19: 6 Lost Treasures Worth Billions (One Was Almost Melted for Scrap)

lines.text: Two thousand feet below the Caribbean Sea lies a ship packed with gold, silver and emeralds. Some say it's worth seventeen billion dollars.
It was found more than ten years ago. And yet, almost all of it is still down there.
That's number one on this list. But first, five other lost treasures that people have hunted for years.
Some were never found. One was found by accident. And one almost got melted down for scrap.
Number six. Poland, August 2015.
For decades, a legend has gone around these mountains. In 1945, a Nazi train loaded with gold rolled into a tunnel, and was never seen again.
Then two treasure hunters went public. They said they'd found it, buried in a hidden tunnel.
They showed a ground radar image. And a government official said he was ninety-nine percent sure the train was real.
The news went around the world. Treasure hunters poured into the town.
But then, scientists from Krakow scanned the hill. Their verdict: there may be a tunnel, but there is no train.
The two men dug anyway, with excavators, in the summer of 2016.
They found no train. Not even a tunnel. Just three holes in the ground, that cost them about thirty-seven thousand dollars.
Number five. Oak Island, Canada.
The story goes that in 1795, a teenager named Daniel McGinnis found a strange dip in the ground, right next to an old oak tree.
He and his friends started digging. And every ten feet or so, they hit a layer of logs. As if someone had built this pit on purpose.
Later diggers claimed they found a stone with strange markings. One reading said: ten feet below, two million pounds are buried.
But every time they got close, the pit flooded with water.
For more than two hundred years, people kept trying. Even a young Franklin D. Roosevelt invested in the hunt, long before he became president.
Six people have died in the search. Four of them in 1965, from poisonous gas in a shaft.
Scientists now think the flooding is natural. And the stone? It's lost.
To this day, no treasure has ever been found. But there's still a TV show about the search, running since 2014.
Number four. Santa Fe, New Mexico, 2010.
An eighty-year-old art dealer named Forrest Fenn fills a small chest with gold coins, gems and jewelry. Worth at least one million dollars.
Then he hides it somewhere in the Rocky Mountains.
The only clue: a twenty-four-line poem in his book, with nine hints.
Thousands of people went looking. They climbed, they dug, they waded through rivers.
And it got dangerous. At least five people died while searching.
Then, after ten years, in June 2020, a thirty-two-year-old medical student named Jack Stuef found it.
Where? In Wyoming. Fenn confirmed it. And just a few months later, he died at the age of ninety.
Number three. Russia, Easter 1887.
Tsar Alexander the Third gives his wife a golden egg made by Faberge. Inside is a tiny watch.
Then came the revolution. The new Soviet government seized the royal treasures, and sold many of them abroad.
The egg disappeared. For decades, nobody knew where it was.
Then, decades later, a scrap metal dealer in the American Midwest spots a gold egg at an antiques market.
He pays about fourteen thousand dollars. His plan: melt it down and sell the gold.
But no one would pay more than he had paid. So he typed the name on the watch into Google.
He found an article about a lost Faberge egg. It looked exactly like his.
Experts in London confirmed it. It was the Third Imperial Egg, reportedly worth around thirty-three million dollars.
He almost melted it. And there are still a few imperial eggs that nobody can find.
Number two. A palace near Saint Petersburg, 1941.
Inside is a room covered in six tons of amber, with gold and mirrors. People called it the eighth wonder of the world.
It was a gift from the king of Prussia to Peter the Great.
Then, the German army invades. In just thirty-six hours, soldiers take the room apart.
They pack it into twenty-seven crates, and ship it to a castle in Konigsberg.
Then the city gets bombed. The castle is left in ruins. And the trail goes cold.
Was it destroyed? Hidden somewhere? Sunk at the bottom of the Baltic Sea? Nobody knows.
Divers even searched a sunken German ship. No amber.
Russia spent twenty-five years and eleven million dollars building a copy. But the original has never been found.
And number one. The Caribbean Sea, June 1708.
A Spanish galleon called the San Jose is sailing toward Cartagena, carrying gold, silver and emeralds from the Americas.
Then, British warships attack.
After about an hour of fighting, the San Jose goes down. Of around six hundred people on board, only about eleven survive.
For three hundred years, the wreck is lost.
Then, in 2015, Colombia announces it has found it. Almost two thousand feet deep.
Cannons. Jars. Piles of coins. Some estimate up to eleven million gold and silver coins.
But who owns it? Colombia says it's theirs. Spain claims it too. American investors want ten billion dollars. And Indigenous people in Bolivia say the treasure was taken from their ancestors.
In 2025, Colombian scientists brought up the first objects. A cannon, a porcelain cup, and three coins.
The rest is still at the bottom of the sea. And the exact spot is a state secret.
So, which treasure would you go looking for? Tell me in the comments. And subscribe to Roundhead Stories for more true money stories.
